subject: Civil Engineering
title: Foundations: Where Bridges Begin
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Foundations: Where Bridges Begin.

hook.text: The Brooklyn Bridge's foundations were dug 78 feet underwater inside airtight boxes.

buildup.text: Caissons — watertight chambers — let workers dig in dry conditions below rivers.

discovery.text: Modern bridges use driven piles or drilled shafts to reach solid rock or firm soil.

twist.text: Scour — river currents washing soil from around piers — is a top cause of failure.

climax.text: Engineers armor foundations with riprap — heavy stones that resist erosion.

punchline.text: A bridge is only as strong as what it stands on.

quiz.question: What is scour in bridge engineering?
options: Rust forming on steel bridge components
River currents eroding soil from around bridge foundations
Wind vibrations that shake the bridge deck

details.summary: Bridge foundations transfer enormous structural loads into the ground or bedrock below. Foundation types include spread footings on strong soil, driven piles through weak soil to rock, drilled shafts bored into bedrock, and caissons sunk through water to riverbed rock.
details.whyItMatters: Foundations are the most critical and often most expensive bridge component. A bridge is only as strong as what it stands on, and foundation failures are among the most catastrophic bridge disasters.
takeaways: Foundation type depends on soil conditions and water depth at each pier
Driven piles transfer loads through friction or by bearing on rock
Caissons are massive chambers sunk to bedrock for major bridges

faq.question: How do engineers determine what foundation type to use for a bridge?
faq.answer: Geotechnical investigations including soil borings, rock core samples, and lab testing reveal subsurface conditions. Engineers match foundation type to soil strength, depth to bedrock, water depth, and construction feasibility. Each pier location may require a different foundation type.

faq.question: What is a caisson and how is it constructed?
faq.answer: A caisson is a large watertight chamber sunk to the riverbed or bedrock to provide a foundation. Open caissons are bottomless boxes sunk by excavating inside them. Pneumatic caissons use compressed air to keep water out during construction. They are used for major bridge piers in deep water.
